reason: The browser-side assembly engine, its view-target and group registries, the retain facet and the React shell are not built. What they did is done on the host: a node registry folds session events into nodes keyed by (kind, id), an index committed with the events finds a node's start, and the same pure functions draw a page and a stream fragment. The package's composer, drafts and recognition of references in sent text are designed by area C3 (areas/ui-chat.md); this area keeps the session page, the composer's place and the regions around it.

The React call tree and the keyed slot tool.call.toolview become a host-rendered card: a frame owned by the conversation area, six closed kinds, and a registry in which the component that owns a tool registers its card by tool name. Cards are still derived from the raw logged call, result and meta, are still pure, and still fall back to the generic card on malformed input.

The question card, its timed wait, the answer bubble and the plan-review card become host-rendered views in one interaction region and in the transcript. The host owns the deadline and the question; forms post to the interaction route; every pending question is listed instead of one at a time; unsent answers stay in the tab.

The approval card that took over the composer becomes a host-rendered card in the interaction region above the composer. It shows what the interaction area lists for a request, offers a session grant only as an explicit non-default choice for an owner and a grantable subject, and is the same item in every tab with the first valid answer winning. Upstream's always-allow button, which was the primary action, is not carried.

The plan chip, the plan cards and the sidebar plan document become a plan control that is shown in both states, a plan card contributed to the end of the turn, a document route that renders the plan from the logged exit_plan_mode call through the safe-HTML renderer, and a review card with approve, request changes and dismiss.

The goal strip becomes a state region beside the composer, drawn from the goal projection and the activation notice, with forms that carry the goal's id and revision and that can also edit the round limit. The bubble that showed a /goal command becomes the general row for every command/run event.

The limit is about upstream's registry of view targets in the browser, where a session renders nothing unless a target such as chat is registered and selected. A server-rendered page has no target registry: the transcript is one compiled view at one URL and the Trajectory view is another page. It exists only because of the React client plugin runtime.

Upstream's conversation content takes its session from where it is rendered, so a second conversation cannot be addressed independently. In the Go design every transcript page, body and region route names the session in its URL path, so any panel can show any session the principal may read.

The Continue action is still offered after a fixed list of failure codes that does not follow the provider's retry settings. The list is the admission rule of the route area (session.prompt with continue=1 and its continuation fold); this area only draws the action when that fold allows it.
justification: A manual action that a person relies on must not appear or disappear when an operator tunes automatic retry, and one more request after a closed stream is harmless. Making the list configurable would add a setting nobody asked for; the page says that continuing may fail again.

reason: The limit describes one rule of upstream's composer style sheet (a backdrop blur under a transformed layer) that was checked only in Chromium. That style sheet belongs to the React composer and is not carried; the Go page specifies no backdrop blur, and visual rules are the design-system area's, tested per supported browser.

Upstream keeps draft attachments as browser objects, so a reload discards them. In the Go design a file is stored on the host when it is added and the draft, a host record, holds the reference (area C3, areas/ui-chat.md, composer.Drafts), so a reload, a session switch and another tab all show the same staged files. This area's page gives the composer one place and never replaces it from the stream.

Upstream lets every mounted attachment view handle a document-level drop, so one drop reaches two composers. The session page declares exactly one composer place per shown session, and area C3's composer rule sends a drop outside a composer to the page's one main composer and to no other.

Upstream replays the whole loaded window whenever one definition fails during an incremental update. The host renderer contains a failing or panicking node definition or card: that one node is drawn as a could-not-render fragment with the event type and sequence number, nothing else is redrawn, and the stream is not closed.

A goal is still session state that survives a change to a preset without goal tools, and the strip can still edit, pause, resume or clear it. The strip now says when the agent's current preset offers no goal tools.
justification: The goal belongs to the session and its service, not to a preset; deleting it on a preset switch would destroy the user's objective, and hiding the strip would remove the only way to pause or clear it. The mismatch is shown instead of hidden.

reason: Upstream's strip cannot raise the round limit, so resuming a goal blocked by its limit fails. The goal form edits the round limit through the same checked service operation the model's tool uses, and a goal blocked by round-limit shows that form. This relies on the goal service's edit operation accepting the limit, listed as a request to area A13.

Upstream's plan mode is guidance only. Area A13 makes it enforced read-only by default (its decision DH-ADR-JOBS-11: a deny-only guard and a read-only sandbox ceiling), and this area's plan control states whether the mode is enforced or guidance, so a person is never told more than is true.

Upstream's chip sits in the default composer, which a pending review replaces. In the Go design the interaction region, the docks and the composer are separate regions, so the plan control stays visible and usable while a plan review or any other interaction is pending.
Upstream shows no control while plan mode is off. The plan control is shown whenever the plan component is loaded: off enters plan mode through the controller with origin ui, on leaves it.

Upstream produces one level of nested calls because run_code is excluded from its own bindings. There is no run_code in the Go design; a script calls tools through the tool command line and each nested call is logged with its parent, so the card frame draws children under their parent to whatever depth the tool pipeline's bound allows.

The limit concerns nested calls recorded by older upstream builds that lack presentation metadata. The Go store reads no upstream session format (DH-ADR-2), and the deferred importer converts only the current format, so no such historical record is ever drawn. It exists only because of upstream's format history.

Upstream keeps the first-party tool views in the one client package. In the Go design the component that owns a tool registers its card by tool name in the card registry; only the frame and the six closed kinds live in the conversation area.

Upstream's tool views get no link callback, so their links ignore the link-opening setting. Every link in rendered content and in a card is written by one helper of the render package with fixed attributes, and with no embedded browser pane (DH-ADR-18) there is one behaviour for an external link everywhere: a new browser tab.

Upstream's tool copy lives in another package's dictionary. A card registered by a tool's owner uses message keys of the owner's own catalogue namespace, and the frame's own text is in this area's namespace, each with English and Chinese complete.

Unsent answers to a question are still kept per tab (fields marked for the page shell's per-tab store), so another browser or device sees the question, which is host state, and not the half-typed answer.
justification: A draft changes on every keystroke and is a convenience of one viewer; the design's rule for view state puts unsent question answers in the per-tab store (DH-ADR-REACT-1). Saving them on the host would cost a request per pause in typing and a merge rule between two people answering one question.

reason: Upstream shows one request in the composer seat and reveals the next only when it resolves. The interaction region lists every pending approval and question of the shown session in ask order, each with its own form.

Upstream shows a pending question only in its own session's composer. The interaction stream event carries the pending items of every session the principal may answer, so the region also names other sessions with something waiting and links to them, and the attention stream raises a notification when no tab shows the session.

Upstream's shared card leaves scope, identity checks and saved grants to each caller, and application consent reuses it with its own always-allow. In the Go design approval outcomes are the interaction area's closed set, a grant is host state that is logged, listed and revocable and never outlives the session, and the consent kind uses the same card with no grant choice.

Final verdict after reading the note: keep its model and move it to the host. Identity taken from the event's own data, one start per (kind, id), a pure fold in sequence order and a definition that owns its node are what make a replay equal the live view, and they do not depend on React. Not carried: contexts held in the browser, pending contexts for a start outside the loaded window (the host has the whole log and an index of starts), predecessor readers, publication cadences and keyed React snapshots.

Final verdict: keep the rule, move the place. The note's point is that reading history must not run presenters, restore scopes or depend on the tool registry, and that a card is derived from the raw call, result and meta where it is drawn. That holds: the store never runs a presenter, and the host's UI layer derives the card at render time from logged facts, by tool name, without a step view or a live agent. The first verdict said the same in outline; the addition is that cards are registered globally so a cold session draws them.

Final verdict: keep the split the proposal wants (a session-owned draft apart from an editor that owns only caret and DOM) and drop its two-stage refactoring plan, which is upstream process. The split is the island rule of the Go design: the host holds the draft record and the island holds nothing authoritative. The composer is designed by area C3 (areas/ui-chat.md); this area fixes the page rules around it.

Final verdict: keep the separation the note argues for (a business grouping rule apart from a generic assembler, one grouping result for every display density) and drop the React identity constraints that shaped its API. In the Go design the rule is area C3's pure reading plan; this area's renderer draws each node into the container the plan names and replaces a group's shell once when the plan closes it.

Final verdict: keep the product behaviour (a new session may be prefilled, an existing draft is kept, replaced or appended to by an explicit rule, and prefilling never sends or runs a command) and replace the mechanism, which is about input-model objects and React mount order. The draft is a host record that the composer fragment is rendered from, so the initial content is in the first response; area C3 designs it.

Final verdict: keep the behaviour (a recognised command is one atomic unit at the start of the draft, deleting it releases the claim and undo restores it) because the note records that styled text looped inside the editor library. The node model belongs to the composer island, which area C3 designs; the host parses the command from the canonical text either way.

Final verdict differs from the first one, which kept the algorithm. The note's evaluator recognises references again each time sent text is shown and caches queries so that a change of facts refreshes little. The Go design does not recognise twice: mention spans are recorded when a message is sent and area C3's usertext view draws them, with credentials masked; a transcript node of this area prints user text only through that view. With nothing re-evaluated there is no cache, no facts dependency and no UTF-16 offset question.

Final verdict: keep as written. A node definition may claim an event so that a generic definition does not also draw it; all matches of an event are evaluated before any is accepted, so the result does not depend on registration order; two claims on one event fail and name both kinds. The shipped use is the same: the reply to a question is drawn by the question-reply node and not also as a plain user message.

Final verdict: the goal stands and the mechanism goes. Upstream holds a session scope alive so that browser-held files survive a switch, and tells the user after a reload that they were discarded. In the Go design a file is stored on the host when it is added and the host-stored draft holds its reference, so a switch, a reload and another tab keep it; nothing has to be held alive in the browser. Area C3 designs the draft record.

Final verdict: keep the feature and its durable form. A quote is plain Markdown quote lines in the sent message, with no source coordinates, which is what makes it survive without its source. The atomic quote node is part of the composer island that area C3 designs; the session-views area supplies the quote and recognise functions; the transcript draws a sent quote through C3's user-text view.

Final verdict: keep the goal and the evidence, move the mechanism. Every chunk is still folded at once, and the visible update is bounded, now by the host: a connection gets at most one live frame per interval, each carrying only new frozen blocks and the tail. The note's 100,000-chunk run becomes a local test with virtual time and a real-browser budget scenario. The animation-frame publication and the React scheduling it worked around do not exist.

title: The transcript is folded on the host by a node registry, and a node is found through an index committed with its events
Placement and folding are area C3's plan; this area draws into it, sends closed work as a summary with a lazy body, and virtualises nothing
A streaming message is one live element, updated in block-level frames and replaced by its settled node in the same stream event
Untrusted text becomes HTML only in the render package: typed parts, a fixed vocabulary, an allow-list gate, and htmx switched off around the result
A remote image is fetched by the host after a click, from the address in the log, through the guarded client
A tool card is a frame owned here plus a closed kind or a body registered by the tool's owner, derived from logged facts at render time
Pending approvals and questions are one state region above the composer, listed in full; a session grant is an explicit choice and never the default
The composer, sent user text and queued input are area C3's design; this area owns the session page, the composer's seat and the regions around it
A session's log is shown as a transcript of nodes, the same from a page load and from the stream
Model and tool text is rendered as safe HTML, and injected markup, script and htmx attributes are inert
A reply is visible while it is written and settles without a flicker, a duplicate or a stale partial
Every tool call is a card with an honest state, bounded output and a readable diff
A remote image in model output loads only after a click
A person answers approvals and questions inline from any tab, and grants or revokes a session grant
Plan mode, plan review, the goal and the task list are visible and controllable beside the composer
Long sessions stay usable: closed work is fetched on demand, any window is drawn directly, and budgets are measured
A page at any cut plus the later event fragments equals the page at the head
Node registry: duplicate kinds, exclusive claims in either order, two claims fail, unloading an owner
The node index finds a start outside the window, reads nothing after the event drawn, and degrades when pending
A failing node definition or card costs one fallback fragment and never closes the stream
Nodes are placed by the reading plan, user text is printed only through the user-text view, and the session page declares its places
A closed process group is a summary with an address and no rows, replaced once, and its body route returns the rows
Rendered output holds only the gate's elements, attributes, classes and address forms, over the corpora and by fuzzing
Hostile markup, script, htmx attributes, region ids and stream-framing text are inert, and gated content is always fenced
Parts: a remote image is a slot and never an img, code is a code part, local links only when settled and under the session prefix
Math is typeset only when settled and falls back to its source on any failure or by setting
Hostile sizes and shapes are bounded or cut, and a renderer panic yields escaped text
Live frames applied in order equal a fresh streaming render; slow and late connections converge
Settlement carries the node and the emptied live element in one fragment, and live state is always released
100,000 reasoning chunks give at most one frame per interval and bytes proportional to the result
Each tool card state from its event sequence, including outcome unknown, a late return and nested calls
Card registry: generic fallback, purity, a cold session needs no agent, golden files for the six kinds
Long output is lazy and paged, a spilled or truncated result says so, a diff folds at nine rows
Image load: the address comes from the log, forbidden destinations and types are refused, one outbound request without cookie or referrer
Approval card content, the grant choice only for an owner and a grantable subject, allow once as default, settlement shown to late answerers
Question forms: answer encoding, the hold, late and second answers, read-only review, draft fields
The grants strip lists and revokes through the grant service, and grant events are transcript rows
Docks: pending values are never drawn as empty, goal forms are compare-and-set, plan control, plan document and review settlements
A window rendered as of a cursor ignores later evidence; jump and tail windows have the right controls
A streamed answer reads the same in two tabs across a network cut and a host restart
Hostile model and tool output is inert in a real browser
A remote image is fetched only after the click, and never from a private address by default
Two browsers see one approval; the first answer wins; a session grant is offered, listed and revoked
Tool cards tell the truth for a real command, a real edit and a hung tool
A timed question, a plan review and a goal are handled from the page
Long sessions and long streams stay within measured budgets
